title: The Joint Commission for Bringing a Friend
subtitle: Native cooperative games, shared puzzles and stories for an optional companion

opening.title: Two Controllers, One Astonishingly Bad Contract
paragraphs: I bought a second controller and announced that loneliness had been defeated. Tank asked where the batteries were. I told him he was focusing on implementation instead of vision. He put the controller down. My victory lasted eleven seconds.

The Joint Commission for Bringing a Friend met at the same table that had survived the other five volumes. Survived was the right word. Its legs had begun making small noises of legal significance. The game binder lay across the middle like a bridge that had been designed by a man who hated rivers. Beside it sat the gold stamp, the tiny red stapler, and a plate of sandwiches Rosa had expressly excluded from all jurisdiction.
I had prepared seats for Player One and Player Two. Player One's seat reclined. Player Two's was a folding chair with a sticker that said AUXILIARY.
Shawna peeled off the sticker.
“Everybody gets a comfortable chair.”
“The design expresses roles.”
“So does a throne. We aren't putting one in the living room.”
Tank looked toward the hallway. I looked somewhere else. The delivery men would be informed.

The reader had asked, at various points, whether a game could be enjoyed together. I had heard an opportunity to establish a commission. Those were not the same request. Mercedes made me write the ordinary question on the first page: what would each person actually do?

That exposed a surprising number of differences. In some games, two people each controlled a character. In some, one character had more abilities than the other. In others, players needed separate devices and had to describe information neither could see in full. Some games offered distinct cooperative levels rather than a shared version of the main story. And some had no native cooperative mode at all; two people could still enjoy discussing a puzzle while one operated the controls.
I had labelled all of these TWO FRIENDS, EXCELLENT. Shawna returned the page with the kind of silence that means a document has disappointed a woman personally.
“We need the distinction,” she said.
“We have a distinction. Excellent is in italics.”
Rosa took the marker from me.

We made three plain signs. Two people controlling the game. Two people sharing ideas around one player's game. A game for somebody who specifically wanted its action demands. The last sign was necessary because friendly art could conceal a lot of running, jumping, aiming, holding, and falling off things. A knitted character could demand excellent timing while looking as if it had personally forgiven you.

Tank recovered the batteries from the drawer marked HISTORICAL RECORDS. The records were mostly spare cables and a receipt for the sign that said I UNDERSTAND. He installed them in the second controller. I watched him perform the practical miracle my announcement had skipped.
“Now,” he said, “who's doing what?”

That became our opening question for every shared game. A helpful friend could handle a menu or read a clue, if invited. A helpful friend could also become a second weather system, shouting instructions while pushing the pace. We agreed to describe before commanding, ask before taking over, and leave space for the person holding the controls to make the interesting decision.
Mercedes tested the arrangement by handing me a sandwich.
“Eat this cooperatively.”
I held one side. Tank held the other. We looked at each other for a while.
“This is stupid,” he said.
“Some activities have a natural lead.”
Rosa cut the sandwich in half. It was the first redesign of the day to improve everybody's experience without a presentation.

The native-co-op label would describe a feature, not a social obligation. Nobody owed us a second player. Nobody needed permission to enjoy a game alone. Where cooperative support depended on an edition, a platform, an update, or a particular mode, we would say so. The original Secret of Mana and its later remake were not one interchangeable object merely because their names matched. My filing cabinet had tried that trick with three different insurance policies. It had not survived contact with Shawna.

We also needed to distinguish a first trial from a promise about the whole game. A pleasant opening could introduce later timers, fights, menus, or demanding movement. Our invitation was to test one useful thing: a conversation between players, a room, a small build, a puzzle, a handoff. We were not scheduling anybody's endurance.
I stamped the revised charter. This time the ink worked. Unfortunately I had placed the charter on the sandwich plate.
“You certified the bread,” Tank said.
I turned the slice over. JOINT COMMISSION shone blue across the crust.
Mercedes leaned back in her comfortable chair. “At least that one actually supports two people.”
We ate the unstamped halves and opened the binder. The second controller remained available. It did not acquire authority over anybody by being present.

games.case_title: The Sword Requires Fewer Speeches and More Attention
scene: I lifted a cardboard sword and announced that the three of us would restore balance to the world. Tank asked whether balance included moving the binder away from the edge of the table. I said the quest had many layers.

Secret of Mana gave us forests, companions and monsters that did not wait for my speeches. I attempted to negotiate with the first creature by explaining our cooperative values. It appeared unmoved by the committee's mission statement.
Shawna reached for the ring menu. For a moment, the action stopped and we could think. I immediately proposed a subcommittee on swords. She closed the menu before I found a chairperson.

Rosa clarified that playing together meant each person actually wanted to fight, explore and manage the party. It did not mean Tank performed every difficult action while I called it leadership. We set down the cardboard sword and agreed to try one familiar area, with both voices carrying more weight than my heroic introduction.
games.pleasure: The original 1993 adventure offers a colourful party journey with native cooperative fighting once companions join. Its overhead view removes free-camera steering, while towns, equipment, magic and connected areas give the journey continuity.
games.burden: Combat runs in real time. Original manual instructions include held dashing and charged attacks, plus Y opening the paused ring menu. Original SNES two-player play needs two controllers; a third needs a multiplayer adapter. Collection of Mana supports up to three. The 2018 remake is excluded.
games.first: Enjoy the solo opening together or use an existing shared save after an ally joins. Try moving, opening the ring and one familiar encounter. The second player should choose their own role rather than automatically receiving every difficult job.
games.ruling: A conditional retro expedition for two willing adventurers; my cardboard sword qualifies only as evidence that packaging can develop delusions.

games.case_title: The Ferry's Emotional Baggage Exceeds My Luggage Allowance
scene: I designed a passenger ferry with a ballroom, a portrait gallery and an extremely small place for passengers. Rosa asked where anyone would sleep. I pointed to a future expansion marked COMFORT, PENDING PRESTIGE.

Spiritfarer had a better order of priorities. People arrived carrying needs, histories and the knowledge that a journey could end. My proposed Captain's Welcome was seven pages long. Tank used page four to level the model boat.

Daffodil the cat had my immediate respect: excellent presence, no committee membership required. I announced that I would take the cat role and supervise from an attractive ledge. Shawna suggested actually testing what the two roles could do before allocating our entire friendship.

We cooked one imaginary meal and removed the ballroom from the plan. Mercedes kept the window seat. The boat was smaller, more useful and considerably less impressed with me. I found that I could bear this, particularly when somebody passed me the bread.
games.pleasure: Build and travel on a ferry, care for spirits, gather materials and eventually say goodbye. The Farewell Edition includes the expanded character stories. Native local cooperation pairs Stella with Daffodil, giving two people a shared place to inhabit.
games.burden: Movement includes jumping and gliding; chores, recipes and resources accumulate. The cat's role differs from Stella's. A previously inspected secondary walkthrough identifies Elena's later timed Gold Dragon challenge, so the gentle presentation is not a no-rush guarantee. Bereavement is the central theme.
games.first: Meet a passenger, walk around the boat and try one chore in each role. Check whether both people enjoy what their character can do. Leave the larger building plan alone until the small shared activity feels worthwhile.
games.ruling: For company that wants to care for a floating household; the committee has denied my application to become Admiral of the Pantry.
games.title: Spiritfarer: Farewell Edition

games.case_title: A Rock Has Been Appointed My Publicist
scene: I volunteered to play the fallen star, for reasons I considered obvious. Tank volunteered to be the rock, for reasons he said were becoming increasingly obvious to everyone else.

Pode asks its unlikely pair to help each other through a mountain. I explained that a star should naturally receive the larger dressing room. Tank pointed out that we were in a cave and neither of us had a dressing room. Shawna gave my imaginary agent a pebble to sit on.

The interesting thing happened when we stopped discussing which character mattered more. One ability opened a possibility the other could use. My magnificent glow was useless in the wrong place; Tank's patient presence had practical consequences.

Rosa watched us rehearse a route with two salt shakers. 'Try asking where he needs you.' I did. For several beautiful seconds, I contributed without announcing a new era. Then I demanded a commemorative photograph, and the rock declined to comment.
games.pleasure: A rock and a fallen star explore Norwegian-inspired caverns, using different abilities to bring an ancient environment to life and solve spatial puzzles. The Switch edition supports one or two players on one system.
games.burden: You still move characters through three-dimensional spaces and coordinate their positions and abilities. The store's cooperative and gentle-looking presentation does not prove no held movement, no tricky jumps or no timed sections throughout. The assigned edition is Switch; PC controller requirements are not imported here.
games.first: Try the first shared room and let each person explain what their character appears able to change. Check movement, positioning and the viewpoint before tackling a long puzzle. Switch roles only if both people would like to.
games.ruling: Recommended conditionally for a pair curious about complementary talents; the rock's refusal to attend my press conference counts as sound geological judgement.

games.case_title: The Farm's First Crop Is an Unnecessary Spreadsheet
scene: I arrived in Stardew Valley with a five-year agricultural strategy and no clear understanding of where I had put the hoe. The first field was assigned to revenue optimisation. The second was reserved for a statue commemorating the first.
Rosa wanted a little garden. Tank wanted to see the town. Mercedes wanted to know why my spreadsheet had already made everyone late for something that had not happened.

The valley contains neighbours, seasons, crops and opportunities to become busy. I interpreted this as permission to run the farm like a minor empire. Shawna placed one seed packet over the spreadsheet and asked what we actually wanted to do together.

We settled on a small patch and a walk. I struggled with the modest scale of our success until a plant became more interesting than my projected margins. The statue remained unbuilt. Several residents benefited from never learning that it had been proposed, which I recorded as a community relations achievement.
games.pleasure: Farming, friendships, seasons, crafting and exploration create a place that can grow alongside a group. The current inspected PC listing advertises online cooperation and shared-screen support, allowing genuine joint work rather than only discussion beside one controller.
games.burden: An active day, energy, inventories, travel, fishing and combat create different demands. Multiplayer pause behavior must be checked; a partner does not automatically stop the clock. Many recipes and social schedules can turn leisure into planning. Record the actual installed version before comparing features.
games.first: Plant a small patch or take one walk together. Inspect movement, item selection and what happens to time when a menu opens. Avoid choosing a mining or fishing challenge as the sole measure of whether village life appeals.
games.ruling: Conditionally welcome when a farm sounds like a place to visit, not another dashboard; my statue may remain theoretical indefinitely.

games.case_title: The Cathedral Has No Door Because I Began with the Spire
scene: I chose Minecraft's Creative mode and began a cathedral dedicated to my own surprisingly modest ambitions. Its spire could be seen from almost anywhere. Its entrance could be seen from nowhere, because I had forgotten to build one.
Tank made a doorway. Rosa made a little seating area. Mercedes added a window that improved the building so much I briefly considered calling it my original intention.

The blocks gave us something to discuss that was neither a score nor my architectural reputation. Shawna tried the camera, placed a few pieces and decided that the movement itself deserved attention before we expanded the project.

I proposed a grand opening. Nobody wanted another ceremony. We sat inside the unfinished structure and looked out of Mercedes's window. The view contained a hill, a tree and no explanation of my achievements. I admitted it was rather good. Tank offered to build a plaque saying AIDEN EVENTUALLY FOUND THE DOOR, but Rosa persuaded him that the doorway already made the point.
games.pleasure: Creative mode supplies unlimited resources, damage immunity and flight for shared building. Java and Bedrock both support multiplayer, but they have different compatibility and input profiles. A modest construction can give two people an enjoyable shared purpose.
games.burden: Moving while steering a three-dimensional view and precisely placing blocks can be substantial work. Creative mode changes survival pressure, not those demands. Official comparison lists controller support for Bedrock, not Java, and split-screen only on consoles; do not plan PC couch split-screen.
games.first: Choose the exact edition and arrange compatible separate-device play if sharing online or locally. In Creative mode, try looking around and placing a few blocks before planning anything large. A wall with one window is an adequate architectural brief.
games.ruling: A conditional building invitation when the camera feels comfortable; all cathedrals must demonstrate a functioning entrance before accepting my name.

games.case_title: The Island Has Elected Somebody Else to Relax
scene: I stepped onto the island and announced a comprehensive beautification programme. First would come a triumphal avenue. Then a plaza. Then a tasteful plaque explaining why the avenue and plaza were named after the same unusually deserving person.
Rosa picked up a shell and said she liked the beach as it was. Tank found somewhere to sit. Mercedes asked whether my plan included a district where nobody had to listen to a plan.

Animal Crossing: New Horizons made room for collecting, decorating and visiting. I tried to convert those possibilities into a compulsory itinerary. Shawna gently returned the itinerary to the binder, where it could inconvenience only the other paper.

We spent a while looking at things. I discovered a particularly excellent spot for a bench and nearly ruined it by calling it an urban planning breakthrough. Instead, I asked who wanted to choose the bench. The island survived this astonishing decentralisation, and my imaginary mayoral sash was repurposed as a ribbon for the picnic basket.
games.pleasure: Collect materials, meet animal neighbours and gradually arrange an island home. The current Switch page supports up to four people sharing one system and larger visits with separate systems, though these are different ways of playing together.
games.burden: Crafting, tool selection, storage and repeated dialogue can create menu work. Same-system roles and restrictions deserve a practical check before assuming everyone has identical freedom. The page reflects current updates, so check the installed version; this card does not certify every activity as untimed.
games.first: Walk around, talk to one neighbour and try placing or collecting an object. If playing together, test the specific visiting or shared-system mode and let both people describe what they can actually do. An unproductive beach stroll is a valid result.
games.ruling: Promising in spirit but conditional in operation: approved for people who want an island, with no requirement to elect me its visionary.

games.case_title: The Test Chamber Has Rejected My Motivational Poster
scene: I brought Portal 2 a motivational poster reading THINK OUTSIDE THE BOX. Tank looked at the test chamber and asked whether I had considered locating the box first.

I proposed that one robot provide inspiration while the other handled buttons, portals and the inconvenient business of survival. Shawna said that sounded suspiciously like our old office arrangement. Mercedes assigned me the next physical task before I could establish a leadership exception.

The pleasure of a cooperative chamber is that two perspectives can become one solution. The less pleasant discovery was that my perspective included repeatedly looking at the wrong ceiling. Tank described the actual panel. I followed his description and, for once, improved the situation.

The poster eventually became a useful diagram on its reverse side. Rosa drew the two portal colours clearly and asked what information each of us needed. We had a plan rather than a slogan. This offended my communications department but worked considerably better.
games.pleasure: The dedicated two-player campaign has its own robots, story and chambers designed around joint portal solutions. Humour and mechanical discoveries make it attractive to companions who like discussing how a space works.
games.burden: First-person movement, aiming, spatial transformations and coordinating actions remain substantial catches. Steam declares play without timed input, but that declaration is not a tested guarantee that every cooperative manoeuvre avoids urgency or awkward timing. Both camera comfort and joint execution need direct trials.
games.first: Enter the cooperative introduction and test looking, walking and placing a portal before pursuing a complex solution. Describe a location without pointing at the other person's screen. Stop if the camera or required coordination outweighs the pleasure of solving.
games.ruling: A conditional laboratory visit for two people who enjoy spatial reasoning; motivational posters must earn their wall space by becoming diagrams.

games.case_title: My Public Relations Department Is Two Geese
scene: I hired two geese to improve the office's public image. The first stole my pen. The second honked during the phrase stakeholder confidence. Their invoice, had they issued one, would have been impeccable satire.

Untitled Goose Game gives two players a village in which to collaborate on mischief. I admired the efficiency of a plan that could be communicated through waddling and the removal of somebody else's hat.

Shawna asked whether I preferred operating the goose or telling everyone where it should go. This was a difficult distinction for a man who had recently called a traffic cone his deputy. Tank took the other role and waited while I examined the surroundings instead of rushing the next prank.

Rosa reminded us that only fictional gardeners were available for harassment. My attempt to honk at the actual kettle received no institutional support. Mercedes returned the stolen pen and gave the geese my job description. They appeared fully qualified.
games.pleasure: The updated PC game lets two people play the whole village prank campaign together. Watching people react, coordinating distractions and creating ridiculous little situations can be as entertaining as completing the written objectives.
games.burden: Stealth, pursuit, object handling and positioning operate in real time. Some tasks require observing routines and acting at a useful moment; held inputs and later time challenges need checking. A charming goose is still capable of making a control scheme demanding.
games.first: Explore the first garden together and try moving, honking and handling one object before attempting an elaborate prank. Agree whether either person wants hints. Enjoy an accidental comic moment without turning every task into a performance target.
games.ruling: Admitted when shared mischief sounds better than shared productivity; the geese have already exceeded my department's annual honesty forecast.

games.case_title: The Leadership Retreat Is Tangled Around a Table Leg
scene: I connected two lengths of yarn to demonstrate the strength of partnership. Within a minute, one was around a chair, the other was under the printer, and my sleeve had become an unofficial third participant.

Unravel Two's little companions face a more beautiful version of the same practical question: how do connected bodies help each other move? I suggested that I could provide vision while Tank provided traction. Tank suggested that I untie the printer.

The game looked like a lovely invitation to cooperate. Shawna kept the movement demands visible: jumping, swinging, running and finding a route together were part of the invitation too. A soft-looking character did not soften every landing.

Rosa brought scissors for our physical demonstration and asked us to stop turning metaphor into a tripping hazard. Mercedes freed my sleeve. The partnership survived, although its first documented success was allowing everyone to reach the snacks without crawling. I considered commissioning a tapestry. The committee advised against more yarn.
games.pleasure: Two Yarnys work through natural and built environments, helping one another across obstacles. Native local cooperation makes the physical connection between characters a direct shared puzzle, with an emotional story running through the journey.
games.burden: This is an active platforming game: jumping, swinging, running and reaction demands are explicit. Coordination can amplify frustration when one person wants a slower pace. Its warmth does not establish an easy route through every chase or challenge; check any assistance options in the actual build.
games.first: In an early safe area, each person should try movement and one simple shared traversal. Ask whether being physically linked feels funny and satisfying or restrictive. Do not make completing a chase the admission test for an enjoyable evening.
games.ruling: A deliberate action detour for companions who want movement as part of the fun; the office printer has declined to become a Yarny.

games.case_title: Eighty Days, Seventy-Nine Hatboxes
scene: I packed for a journey around the world with one useful coat and seventy-nine containers of ceremonial importance. Tank asked what was in the largest box. I said the smaller boxes needed a dignified entrance.

In 80 Days, routes, money, luggage and a companion's needs make travel a sequence of interesting compromises. My first proposed itinerary involved visiting every city that might appreciate my hat. Shawna calculated that this would take substantially longer than the wager allowed.
Mercedes wanted to follow an intriguing conversation. Rosa wanted to know whether we could afford the next connection. Both concerns proved more engaging than my luggage manifesto.

We reduced the baggage and chose a direction together. Nobody pretended the decision had become certain merely because two people discussed it. I retained one excellent hat and discovered that an unexpected encounter could justify a detour. Tank carried the map, largely to prevent me replacing the continents with a diagram of my personal brand.
games.pleasure: As Passepartout, choose routes and encounters across an alternate-history world while managing Fogg's wellbeing, money and travel. This is single-player storytelling that can be discussed beside the screen; its shared appeal does not make it native cooperative play.
games.burden: The premise includes a travel deadline, schedules and an in-game clock. The inspected store language stresses continuous time, so do not assume a fully untimed experience or confuse the multiplayer journey feed with joint control. Reading, inventory and route planning are significant.
games.first: Inspect the opening route choices and how time behaves in each screen before committing to a journey. Let the person operating choose whether advice is welcome. One interesting encounter is enough to assess the prose and decision rhythm.
games.ruling: Conditionally approved for armchair travellers who enjoy a consequential itinerary; my hatboxes may circle the globe separately at their own expense.

games.case_title: My Future Self Has Misfiled the Past
scene: I offered to be the future in The Past Within because I felt my achievements belonged there. Tank accepted the past on condition that he would not be held responsible for anything I eventually did with the stationery budget.
Our two screens did not contain the same information. I began describing a symbol as a triumphant shape of inevitable progress. Shawna asked whether it was a triangle. It was a triangle.

The puzzle improved when I stopped narrating my importance and started reporting useful details. Tank told me what he saw. I repeated it back. For a remarkable moment, neither of us accused the other of having the wrong screen.

Rosa supplied paper for notes; Mercedes vetoed a twenty-page communication protocol. The spooky Vanderboom mystery continued without our administrative assistance. I did, however, send a warning to my future self about leaving biscuit crumbs in the keyboard. The future offered no assurances, which seemed entirely consistent with its record so far.
games.pleasure: Two players occupy different times and exchange information to solve a Rusty Lake mystery. Separate perspectives make describing, listening and comparing observations the actual cooperative activity rather than a decorative addition to a solo puzzle.
games.burden: This is co-op only: each player needs their own copy, a device and a way to communicate. Eerie imagery and puzzling symbols may be unwelcome. Reading, remembering descriptions and manipulating the interface still need checking; the premise does not establish a complete absence of timed or held actions.
games.first: Set up both perspectives and exchange one precise observation before pursuing a solution. Try any unfamiliar interaction separately. Decide whether the pleasure comes from explaining what you see, and whether either person wants brief written notes.
games.ruling: Approved conditionally for a pair who enjoy saying what is actually on their screens; triumphant shapes of inevitable progress should first be checked for three sides.

games.case_title: Kirby Inhales My Entire Presentation
scene: I had just reached slide seventeen when Kirby inhaled the projector. This was not a feature I could promise from the actual game, but as a fantasy of office reform it held obvious merit.

Kirby and the Forgotten Land offered us an overgrown world and two different roles. I wanted to be the star. Tank wanted to know which role allowed him to get on with the game while I explained that desire.

Shawna put the controllers down long enough to settle it properly. One person could play Kirby, the other Bandana Waddle Dee; the characters were not interchangeable job titles. Mercedes suggested we try both before I established a constitutional monarchy.

Rosa liked the town and wanted time to look around. The adventure also contained fights and challenges. We agreed that the pinkness of the hero was not evidence about the difficulty of every action. My slides were quietly retired. Kirby received credit for a productivity improvement he had achieved only inside my extremely selective imagination.
games.pleasure: Explore three-dimensional stages, rescue Waddle Dees and develop a town between adventures. Original Switch local cooperation adds Bandana Waddle Dee beside Kirby. Nintendo's Spring-Breeze mode gives more health and easier enemies.
games.burden: This remains platforming and combat. Nintendo explicitly describes timed Treasure Road challenges and abilities involving held buttons, such as charging a hammer or aiming a bomb. The second role differs. The 2022 Switch original is assessed here, not the Switch 2 expansion or upgrade.
games.first: Try the opening area in Spring-Breeze mode if desired, testing movement and each character's basic actions. Check whether both people like their role before pursuing a boss or time challenge. The official page lists a demo, whose current availability can be checked on the console.
games.ruling: A conditional expedition when active movement sounds appealing; the committee cannot legally list projector consumption as an accessibility option.

games.case_title: Four Kirbys Apply for the Same Corner Office
scene: Once I learned we could have several Kirbys, I declared the corner office insufficiently cornered. Four distinguished heroes would require four distinguished views. Tank rotated the table and said the problem was solved.

Return to Dream Land Deluxe gives a group more character choices than my original seating plan. I announced that everyone could choose freely, then delivered a speech about why my preferred choice naturally carried executive authority.
Shawna selected a character before the speech finished. Mercedes selected another. Rosa asked whether the little cosmic traveller needed his ship repaired or merely a committee to discuss the damage.

The actual adventure required moving, fighting and helping. It also offered Helper Magolor, which seemed a better practical resource than my motivational remarks. I tried to appoint myself Helper Aiden. Tank handed me the refreshments and told me I had finally identified a useful role. The ship remained fictional, but the tea arrived at a sensible temperature and without a ceremonial launch.
games.pleasure: The Deluxe Switch platform adventure supports up to four local players, including different Kirbys and familiar companions. Repairing Magolor's ship gives the group a shared journey, while character abilities and separate subgames provide variety.
games.burden: Floating, fighting, jumps and different move sets remain active demands. Nintendo confirms Helper Magolor for the main adventure, but that does not erase every challenge. The later Magolor Epilogue must be unlocked and has its own action; do not treat all modes as equivalent.
games.first: Use an early main-adventure section to test movement and a character's basic ability. Examine Helper Magolor if helpful. Leave competitive subgames and coordinated team attacks for later, and keep the first shared session free from a completion target.
games.ruling: Conditionally suitable for a group that wants colourful action with some assistance; four Kirbys do not require four separate speeches about my chair.

games.case_title: The Flower Has More Stage Presence Than I Do
scene: I entered the Flower Kingdom prepared to be the most surprising object in the room. A talking flower immediately challenged that assumption. Then the landscape began doing things my planning documents had failed to anticipate.

Super Mario Bros. Wonder seemed determined to make curiosity physical. I attempted to preserve my dignity by explaining every new transformation as if I had personally authorised it. Mercedes asked me to let the surprise finish before taking credit.

Shawna considered the different characters. Nabbit and Yoshis avoided enemy damage, which sounded useful, but the courses still needed moving through. Tank asked whether I understood the difference between protection and the ground continuing beneath one's feet. My recent relationship with the office step stool suggested further research.

Rosa chose the character she liked. We agreed to travel at a pace the group could actually share. I put away the stopwatch I had brought for my triumphal entrance, and the talking flower continued its career without needing to chair a single meeting.
games.pleasure: Side-scrolling courses change in imaginative ways when Wonder effects appear. Up to four local players can tackle them together. Nabbit and Yoshis avoid damage from enemies, and Yoshis can carry other players.
games.burden: Running, jumping, gaps, moving hazards and coordination remain part of an action game. Enemy-damage protection does not certify an effortless or no-hold path through every course. Character restrictions also matter: Nintendo says Nabbit and Yoshis do not transform with power-ups.
games.first: Pick characters for their actual appeal and try one early course without collecting every optional item. Check movement and jump controls before introducing extra badges. A companion should match the agreed pace rather than racing ahead to demonstrate expertise.
games.ruling: A cheerful conditional action choice when surprises and jumps are welcome; the flower's speaking engagement has priority over my ribbon-cutting ceremony.

games.case_title: Two Clocks and One Man Who Cannot Describe a Drawer
scene: I opened the clockmaker's mystery with the confidence of somebody who owned a watch he did not know how to adjust. Tank was given the other screen and immediately encountered information I did not have.
I described a drawer as antique, purposeful and carrying the weight of untold history. Shawna asked whether it was open. It was not. She asked what was on it. I had somehow omitted that part.

Tick Tock: A Tale for Two rewarded the details my dramatic training usually treated as beneath notice. A mark, a position, a sequence: these could help another person. My atmospheric interpretation could wait until we had located the relevant object.

Mercedes established a temporary ban on the phrase time itself. Rosa said either of us could ask for a description again without making it a test. We began to work together. I still admired the watch on my wrist, although it remained impressively accurate about a completely different hour.

games.case_title: I Have Rewound the Meeting but the Minutes Still Embarrass Me
scene: I wanted a way to revisit a meeting and improve the moment when I called the printer a sentient strategic partner. The Gardens Between offered time manipulation, although unfortunately only inside its own carefully designed world.

Arina and Frendt moved among oversized objects from their shared past. I proposed assigning every office object a dramatic memory. Tank picked the broken stapler and recalled the day I bought a replacement that was too small to staple anything.

The puzzles invited us to think about sequence: what changes when time moves one way, and what becomes possible when it moves back? Shawna watched the relationships between objects while Mercedes noticed the feeling of the scene.

Rosa said the friendship mattered more than whether we solved everything quickly. The developer's explicit absence of time pressure supported that approach. I rewound my imaginary meeting again and tried saying less. Everyone agreed this was a promising revision, although the printer's alleged strategic status would remain in the archive forever.
games.pleasure: Manipulate time through dreamlike island scenes built from two friends' memories. The publisher explicitly describes a single-player game with no text, speech or time pressure, giving shared observation room to focus on images and sequences.
games.burden: You control the flow of time rather than simply steering each friend independently. Understanding cause and sequence can still be demanding, and sustained input to move time needs a direct check. Simple controls do not automatically mean no holds. This is shared thinking beside one player, not native co-op.
games.first: Move time forward and back in the opening scene, noticing one object that changes or interacts differently. Check how the input feels before pursuing a long sequence. Decide whether the visual friendship story gives the puzzle enough emotional interest.
games.ruling: Promising when watching a small memory become a mechanism sounds appealing; my printer's executive title cannot be removed through ordinary calendar adjustment.

games.case_title: The Tentacle Has a Better Succession Plan Than I Do
scene: A purple tentacle announced an ambition to take over the world, and I was forced to admit that the competition for ridiculous authority had become serious. Mine had so far reached only the cupboard above the kettle.

Day of the Tentacle put three friends in different times. I immediately saw a chance to send my unfinished paperwork into the past. Shawna asked whether I understood that this might simply make it overdue for longer.

Tank wanted to know what an object could do in another era. Mercedes noticed a visual joke. Rosa asked whether we could follow one thread without opening every inventory at once. These were all better questions than my proposal to appoint a Deputy Director of Yesterday.

We tried to understand one cause and its distant effect. A funny solution became visible when we stopped insisting that objects obey ordinary office logic. I sent no paperwork through time. The tentacle's world-conquest application remained under review, primarily because it had arrived without the correct stationery.
games.pleasure: A cartoon adventure links three protagonists across time, turning changes in one era into possibilities in another. The Remastered edition offers revised art and audio alongside classic presentation options, with comedy built into the puzzle logic.
games.burden: Inventories, character switching and consequences across different periods create a real memory burden. Cartoon logic may feel inventive or arbitrary. The source does not establish every timing or hold demand; preview the interface and selected presentation rather than assuming a classic adventure is automatically easy.
games.first: Explore an early room and identify one useful object or conversation. Try switching the presentation if you prefer, then decide whether the humour and inventory handling appeal. A companion can keep one current question visible without delivering the whole solution.
games.ruling: Conditionally approved for people amused by consequences arriving centuries late; my overdue paperwork is forbidden from using the time machine.

games.case_title: The Wizard Has Built a Box Around My Management Style
scene: I chose the wizard because creating objects from thin air seemed close to my usual budgeting method. Tank chose the knight. Mercedes asked whether anybody had remembered the actual puzzle before selecting a profession.

Trine bound different abilities into one adventure. I summoned an imaginary box and announced that leadership had provided the necessary infrastructure. Shawna pointed out that I had placed it directly in everyone's way.

The thief could approach a space differently; the knight could handle dangers my splendid box did nothing to discourage. Rosa suggested that roles should follow what people enjoyed doing, rather than whichever title best matched my jacket.

We moved the box. This produced a route, a useful metaphor and the first genuine improvement my magic department had delivered all morning. I offered a speech about complementary strengths. Tank lifted the box again and looked meaningfully at me. I understood that cooperation sometimes meant leaving enough room for the other characters, both on the path and in the conversation.
games.pleasure: Wizard, knight and thief combine different abilities in a fantasy world of physical puzzles and combat. Enchanted Edition supports up to three players locally or online, and the original 2009 release is also included as a separate launcher choice.
games.burden: Platforming, fighting, aiming and grappling remain active demands, with different burdens by character. The inspected description declares saving options and the store lists adjustable difficulty, but neither establishes a no-reflex or no-hold path. Choose Enchanted Edition deliberately rather than mixing its features with the original.
games.first: In an early section, try each preferred character's movement and one ability. Discuss whether roles feel satisfying before combining them under pressure. A companion should not become the compulsory combat department unless that is genuinely the role they want.
games.ruling: A deliberate fantasy-action detour for a group that enjoys physical puzzles; boxes bearing my departmental logo must demonstrate that they are not blocking the exit.

games.case_title: The Traveller Has Declined My One Correct Solution
scene: I approached Pilgrims with an official sequence of events. First, meet a traveller. Second, assign the traveller a purpose. Third, demand a progress report before the traveller had finished sitting down.

The game preferred play. An object or character might produce an unexpected response, and different solutions could be part of the pleasure. Mercedes tried something simply because it looked funny. My schedule shuddered but remained technically printable.

Tank offered a new rule: if an experiment made us laugh, we were allowed to count it as something that happened. Shawna pointed out that this was not even a rule, merely an accurate description of enjoying a game.

Rosa gave the imaginary traveller a place at the table without requiring a completed objective. I revised my sequence to begin with See What Happens. This was so alarmingly short that I nearly added an appendix. The tiny red stapler, placed on the blank paper, restrained me more effectively than several previous policy committees.
games.pleasure: A playful illustrated adventure encourages trying items and characters in different situations, with multiple solutions rather than one fixed route through every task. Its brief, expressive reactions can be enjoyable to discover with someone watching beside you.
games.burden: Interpreting unusual responses and managing available objects still requires attention. Test how cards or items are selected and moved; do not assume that a playful interface avoids dragging or held actions. games.first: Try a couple of early combinations and watch what happens without demanding immediate progress. Check whether manipulating the items feels comfortable. A companion can suggest an experiment, but the person playing gets to choose which curiosity to follow.
games.ruling: Promising for people who like a story that tolerates a little messing about; the committee has authorised See What Happens and denied its appendix.

games.case_title: Two Universes Have Both Misplaced My Reservation
scene: I booked an imaginary journey between parallel worlds and requested a suite in each. The first world had no record of me. The second had apparently heard about the first and decided to maintain the policy.

April Ryan's adventure offered a much better reason to travel: people, puzzles and the uneasy relationship between different realities. I began drawing a map that reserved the centre for my portrait. Shawna moved the portrait to the margin so the worlds could actually fit.

Tank asked which conversation we wanted to follow next. Mercedes wanted time with the atmosphere. Rosa said a long story could be visited in pieces rather than swallowed as a demonstration of commitment.

I put the map down and listened. The older presentation asked for a little patience, but patience was not the same as an obligation to tolerate an uncomfortable interface. We agreed to check that first. My suite remained unavailable in both universes, which I described as remarkably consistent cross-dimensional customer service.
games.pleasure: April Ryan moves between parallel universes in a substantial original PC adventure filled with conversations, places and puzzles. Its appeal is spending time with a large imaginative world; another person can share the story and discuss clues beside the player.

games.case_title: The Talking Spoon Has Requested a Different Destiny
scene: A talking spoon seemed a natural addition to my office, where several silent objects already carried more responsibility than their job descriptions allowed. I appointed it Deputy Minister of Breakfast before asking whether it wanted the position.

Broken Age's two young protagonists had their own reasons to question the lives arranged for them. Mercedes looked at the spoon's appointment letter and asked whether I had understood that part of the premise.

Shawna suggested we follow one character's situation first. Tank wanted to test an object interaction rather than sit through my address on destiny. Rosa asked the spoon what it would like for breakfast, which was an odd question but at least granted it some agency.

We switched perspectives and found a world stranger than my office, although considerably better painted. I withdrew the appointment letter. The spoon remained on the table by choice, or at least without written evidence to the contrary. My own destiny involved washing it after lunch, a role with unusually clear responsibilities.
games.pleasure: Vella and Shay navigate very different worlds while trying to take control of their lives. The complete two-act point-and-click adventure combines hand-drawn scenes, voice performances, odd characters and puzzles, with switching between the protagonists part of the structure.
games.burden: Two story threads and inventory reasoning can require remembering details across scenes. Later puzzle complexity should not be inferred from an approachable opening. The developer page supports the premise and point-and-click form, not a full no-timer or no-hold certification. This is shared viewing of a single-player adventure.
games.first: Hear an opening conversation, try one interaction and look at the character-switching interface. Choose which story to follow by interest. A companion can remember an earlier clue without taking over every decision or explaining a solution before it is wanted.
games.ruling: Conditionally welcome for someone who likes imaginative characters questioning their assigned roles; the spoon's ministerial appointment has been rescinded with full washing privileges.

games.case_title: The Crocodile Has Rejected My Welcome Pack
scene: I arrived in Dinkum with a town charter, a decorative shovel and a welcome pack for the local wildlife. Tank asked whether the wildlife had agreed to a town. I said consultation would follow the ribbon cutting.

The game combined building a settlement with a landscape that could be beautiful and dangerous. I attempted to admire a creature on behalf of the tourism department. Shawna suggested admiring it from somewhere less likely to become lunch.

Mercedes wanted to design a pleasant place to live. Rosa wanted the daily tasks to stay manageable. Both intentions seemed more useful than my plan to name every building before we had gathered its materials.

We started small and kept an eye on what survival actually required. I put the wildlife welcome packs back in the binder. The crocodile, as far as our imaginary correspondence established, preferred a more direct approach to visitors. Tank proposed making this fact the town's first piece of useful public information.
games.pleasure: Explore, gather, farm and build a settlement in an Australian-inspired landscape, meeting residents and inviting friends online. The full PC release combines town creation with survival and also includes a separate Creative Mode, offering a different focus for building.

Official launch notes leave some town quests to the host. Record the installed version rather than relying on old Early Access advice.
games.first: Try walking, looking around and one modest town task before entering dangerous terrain. Inspect Creative Mode if building is the attraction, then check the chosen multiplayer permissions. Ask whether both players enjoy their available tasks rather than assigning one all the work.

games.case_title: The Carrots Have Continued Growing Without My Supervision
scene: I left Farm Together for a moment and returned to the shocking possibility that the farm had continued existing without my strategic attention. I had not approved this independence. The carrots appeared entirely unmoved.

Time advancing while we were away could mean a pleasant return to something ready for attention. I tried to convert it into a compulsory check-in schedule. Rosa removed the schedule and said crops in a game were not entitled to summon us from dinner.

Tank liked the possibility of doing a little work side by side. Mercedes wanted a farm with paths that led somewhere attractive, rather than directly to my proposed founder's pavilion. Shawna checked the visiting permissions before imagining a shared project.

We planned a modest patch and an equally modest return. The tractor was allowed to remain a tool rather than a symbol of my agricultural authority. I still asked the carrots for a report. Their continued silence was both insubordinate and, according to everyone else, an excellent influence on the office.
games.pleasure: Grow crops, keep animals, decorate a farm and invite other players to cultivate it together. The first Farm Together explicitly lets time progress while you are offline, creating a place that can be revisited rather than requiring continuous attendance.
games.burden: Repeated tending, expansion, currencies, waiting and item menus can become a workload. Movement and camera handling need a direct check. Online farm permissions matter when sharing; the source does not establish every activity as untimed or hold-free. This card covers the first game, not its sequel.
games.first: Plant or tend one small area and inspect how a friend joins and what they may change. Try camera movement and a basic interaction. Decide whether returning to growing things feels pleasant without agreeing to an attendance schedule.
games.ruling: Conditionally welcome for companions who like a persistent shared garden; the carrots' refusal to attend my progress meeting is fully protected.

games.case_title: The Village Has Built a House Where My Master Plan Used to Be
scene: For the final farm proposal, I promised to listen before producing a master plan. This was easy for almost twelve seconds. Then I saw a flat patch of ground and began mentally arranging a ceremonial avenue.

Staxel let us shape a blocky village, restore a farm and work alongside friends. Tank wanted a useful workshop. Rosa wanted somewhere welcoming. Mercedes wanted to choose the colours herself, a terrifying but constitutionally sound development.

Shawna tested the movement and building controls before granting my imaginary planning permission. A first-person world required looking and moving, even if the activity was domestic. We agreed that a pleasant project could still be the wrong fit for a particular evening.

I set down the plan. Somebody put up a wall; somebody else noticed where a window should go. The little house became a record of choices made together rather than evidence that I had arrived first. I offered to carry the furniture. For once, nobody needed to revise my job description.
games.pleasure: Restore a farm, meet villagers and alter a voxel world through building and cultivation. The PC game explicitly supports online cooperation, allowing friends to share a farm or become neighbours while making their own projects.
games.burden: First-person movement, camera steering, selecting materials, crafting and placing blocks can create substantial coordination and menu demands. Farming tasks add routine work. The publisher's creative premise does not certify no holds, no timed activities or a frictionless multiplayer setup.
games.first: Try looking around, moving through a doorway and placing or interacting with a simple object. If sharing online, establish who owns the session and how both people join. Choose one small project only after the controls feel worth using.
games.ruling: A conditional final invitation for people who enjoy making a place together; my master plan has become spare paper, and the house is better for it.

interludes.title: The Friend Who Became a Tutorial
paragraphs: I discovered an extraordinary gift for cooperative instruction. Whatever Tank was doing, I could describe how I would have done it three seconds earlier. This service required no controller and, apparently, no correct information.
“Go left,” I said.
He went left.
“Your other left.”
Tank paused the discussion by looking at me. It was not a pause button; it was a face. The distinction mattered because I had already become confident enough to promise features I had not checked.
Shawna put a small card beside the screen. It read ASK.
“Ask what?”
“Whether he wants help.”
“He clearly needs—”
She tapped the card.

I asked. Tank said he wanted to try the thing. So I let him try the thing. A door opened. I immediately felt the urge to explain that his method had been broadly consistent with my strategy. Mercedes placed a sandwich directly in my hand. It was a merciful intervention.

Later, in a different puzzle, Tank asked what I could see. I described a shape, its position, and the marks beside it. He compared those with his own information. For once my mouth was connected to an actual function. We made progress by building a shared description, not by making one person into the other's remote-control accessory.
Rosa noticed the difference first. “You two sound like you're enjoying it.”
I wanted to issue a certificate. Shawna pointed at the ASK card. I did not ask whether they wanted a certificate because some impulses deserve to be carried privately until they pass.

We adjusted the room instead. The screen moved so both people could see. A lamp stopped reflecting across a clue. The water came closer. None of that changed the software, and none magically erased a game's real demands. It simply removed three problems I had accidentally supplied for free.

The binder contained some excellent candidates for shared thinking that were still single-player games. We kept that plain. Taking turns at a puzzle could be enjoyable, but it was not the same as two simultaneous characters. Watching a friend play could be a pleasure, but it was not automatically participation. A guest could prefer to watch, offer a theory, take a turn, or go make tea. The room could accommodate all four without assigning ranks.
The red stapler disappeared during this discussion. I suspected theft. Rosa found it beneath my elbow.
“You are the obstacle in more systems than you realize,” she said.
I returned it to its tray. Then I moved my elbow, my advice, and my magnificent self far enough back that the next person could reach the controls.

ending.title: The Commission Votes to Leave the Door Open
paragraphs: The final vote concerned what the commission should do next. I had prepared three options: expand, establish a regional office, or expand while establishing a regional office. Mercedes wrote PLAY SOMETHING in the margin. It won unanimously.
“I haven't voted,” I said.
“You announced the vote was unanimous before you printed the ballot,” Shawna said.
The evidence was in my handwriting. We accepted the result.

Forty entries had given us several different kinds of company. Two characters sharing a world. Two people describing separate clues. A friend watching an absurd scene. A quiet debate over a railway route. A building project that could become a pleasant afternoon or a second job. The useful question remained the one we had started with: what would each person actually do, and would they enjoy doing it?

That question also permitted no. A game could be beautiful and still ask for movement somebody did not want. A cooperative mode could be generous and still give one person a role they found dull. A friend could be dear and still offer far too many instructions. In the last case, I recommended sandwiches as an interim measure and listening as the longer-term repair.
Tank put the second controller beside the first. He did not hand it to anybody. That small decision made the invitation feel different. There it was if wanted. Nothing in the room demanded an answer.
Rosa cleared the plate. She found the stamped slice of bread under my notes.
“Are we preserving this?”
“Founding document.”
“Compost.”
We had a brief constitutional discussion, which the bread lost.

I lifted the enormous binder from the table. Everybody watched, perhaps expecting the building to sigh with relief. It was heavier than any ordinary answer to what to play should have been. That was part of the joke. The real route through it could still be tiny: choose one interesting game, read the catch, try one meaningful thing, and decide whether to continue. The rest was optional company.

Shawna took half the weight. Tank opened the cabinet. Mercedes moved the shelf that I had installed upside down several volumes earlier. Rosa insisted that the snacks remain outside the filing system. Together we found a place for the book that did not require anyone to hold it indefinitely.
The gold stamp went in a drawer. The tiny red stapler stayed on the table. I left the ASK card beside it, where I would see it before developing another policy.
“So what are you now?” Mercedes asked.
I considered Director Emeritus of Recreational Companionship. It had a nice shape. It could fit on a brass plate. It could also turn a quiet evening into another delivery appointment.
“Available,” I said.
Tank nodded. “Good. Bring the water.”

I brought the water. No one applauded. Nobody needed to. The game was already interesting, the chairs were comfortable, and for once the administration had improved the evening by getting out of its way.
